// Pre-filter both ASIM tables before the union — same pattern as the
// Defender version so the engine can push hash predicates per-side.
let BadHashes = dynamic(["021666417de8b9972c179783fe60d4c4ad2d93224e3a0f16137065c960b1b845", "363923500ce942bf1a953e8a4e943fbf1fb1b5ed6e5d247964c345b3ad5bfc34", "8421c902364980e3d762ec6dbbe6b0f40577c27bd79b48c57d098328b2533109", "644fc49fa1006a2a2acace694e5fb83753164e2617051ece6d9dc9ea32329e70", "9053e8ddaecca1f960c041c944ca8799fc71dc86a4b50d2639ee4e0d2cb82f47", "b60074d1ea2008a581f432f2dee5f84f78668d9dd8e66f75d03c42dabd89bdea", "9425e8e39fa8a7212cdd07f0917cb3dfde38a90b87297de2c82a5850aff1e4de", "30448686ec900d5213d74f08f0d2b7924c5336a29445b2a434aba8d8b19d7530", "48047c34bfd57fe1e24bc538bc2ce9e0ac4c4eb48d3b0c195b414f0379dc0745"]);
union
    ( ImFileEvent
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where TargetFileSHA256 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileSHA1 in~ (BadHashes)
           or TargetFileMD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType,
                  TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256,
                  Cmd = ActingProcessName, Source = "ImFileEvent" ),
    ( ImProcessCreate
        | where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
        | where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
        | where SHA256 in~ (BadHashes) or SHA1 in~ (BadHashes) or MD5 in~ (BadHashes)
        | project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, EventType = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileName = TargetProcessName, TargetFilePath = TargetProcessName,
                  TargetFileSHA256 = SHA256,
                  Cmd = TargetProcessCommandLine, Source = "ImProcessCreate" )
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Fake Sites Mimicking Open-Source Tools Rank High on Google to Deliver Malware via TDS

The Hacker News
2026-06-04 15 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have flagged a large-scale operation that impersonates open-source and freeware projects to funnel unsuspecting users through a Traffic Distribution System (TDS) and deliver malware families like Remus Stealer, AnimateClipper, and the SessionGate framework. "The sites are well-designed and often look like legitimate project portals at a glance, sometimes referencing

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Outbound contact to fake open-source tool / TDS / CloudFront staging domains · [LLM] Browser-spawned executable/installer drop within 5 min of TDS site contact · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AnimateClipper ClickFix paste-to-run via explorer.exe spawning mshta/powershell/cmd · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SessionGate final-stage rundll32 spawning cmd.exe to fetch and silently execute next-stage payload · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Remus/Lumma Stealer browser-credential and crypto-wallet directory enumeration · Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Outbound contact to fake open-source tool / TDS / CloudFront staging domains AIDelivery High
Detects host or browser contact (DNS or HTTP) with the eight typosquatted Ghidra/dnSpy/SpiderFoot/grpcurl lookalike sites and the CloudFront-hosted staging layer + downstream TDS endpoints used to deliver SessionGate, Remus Stealer and AnimateClipper. Rationale: Eight domains pulled verbatim from the Check Point breakdown / pre-extracted IOC block (grpcurl.com, ghidralite.com, two CloudFront staging hosts, plus four TDS endpoints). All are confirmed by Check Point and the November 2025 Fullstory write-up referenced in the article body — high-fidelity atomic IOCs. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/ • https://www.fullstory.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1583.008 T1608.006 T1189
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel analyst sandbox detonations of the campaign
  • Security researcher visiting the sites for write-up purposes
  • Legacy bookmark from a stale post linking the typosquatted Ghidra domain
  • Automated link-checker / Safe-Browsing crawler hosted on a corporate egress
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("smartscreen.exe","MsMpEng.exe","NisSrv.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pivot on DeviceName/SrcHostname to identify the user and the parent process; check if a file dropped into Downloads/Temp within 5 min of the contact and pull the SHA256. 2) Contain: isolate the host via EDR, force-revoke active browser sessions for that user, reset all stored browser-saved passwords and 2FA tokens (Remus targets these), and block the eight domains at proxy / firewall. 3) Hunt: sweep the org for the same SHA256, the same CloudFront staging hosts, and any rundll32→cmd.exe chains spawned by the dropped DLL over the next 14 days.

DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where RemoteUrl has_any (TDSDomains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName=InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
let TDSDomains = dynamic(["grpcurl.com","ghidralite.com","dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net","d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net","oundhertobeconisist.org","trkscope.xyz","file-enter-web.com","realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster"]);
union isfuzzy=true
( ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where Url has_any (TDSDomains) or DstHostname has_any (TDSDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname, SrcUsername, Url, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, HttpRequestHeaderUserAgent ),

  | where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
  | where DnsQuery has_any (TDSDomains)
  | project TimeGenerated, SrcHostname=DvcHostname, DnsQuery, SrcUsername )
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: TDS / Fake Open-Source Tool Site DNS or HTTP Contact
id: 7a3e2a1c-9b1d-4c2a-9b8f-fa1c3e4d5b6a
description: Detects DNS/HTTP contact with domains used by the CloudFront-hosted TDS distributing SessionGate, Remus Stealer and AnimateClipper via fake Ghidra/dnSpy/SpiderFoot/grpcurl lookalike sites.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/fake-sites-mimicking-open-source-tools.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.t1583.008
  - attack.t1608.006
  - attack.t1189
logsource:
  category: dns
detection:
  selection:
    QueryName:
      - 'grpcurl.com'
      - 'ghidralite.com'
      - 'dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net'
      - 'd3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net'
      - 'oundhertobeconisist.org'
      - 'trkscope.xyz'
      - 'file-enter-web.com'
      - 'realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster'
  condition: selection
level: high
(source:windows.sysmon @EventID:(3 OR 22)) AND (@DestinationHostname:(*grpcurl.com OR *ghidralite.com OR dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net OR d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net OR *oundhertobeconisist.org OR *trkscope.xyz OR *file-enter-web.com OR *realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster) OR @QueryName:(grpcurl.com OR ghidralite.com OR dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net OR d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net OR oundhertobeconisist.org OR trkscope.xyz OR file-enter-web.com OR realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster))
#event_simpleName=DnsRequest DomainName=/^(grpcurl\.com|ghidralite\.com|dcbbwymp1bhif\.cloudfront\.net|d3jzqhqvnvdy34\.cloudfront\.net|oundhertobeconisist\.org|trkscope\.xyz|file-enter-web\.com|realcubeoyogenmyfire\.monster)$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, DomainName, ContextImageFileName], function=count())
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats summariesonly=t count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Web WHERE (Web.url IN ("*grpcurl.com*","*ghidralite.com*","*dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net*","*d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net*","*oundhertobeconisist.org*","*trkscope.xyz*","*file-enter-web.com*","*realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster*")) BY Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count, min(_time) as firstTime, max(_time) as lastTime FROM datamodel=Web WHERE (Web.url IN ("*grpcurl.com*","*ghidralite.com*","*dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net*","*d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net*","*oundhertobeconisist.org*","*trkscope.xyz*","*file-enter-web.com*","*realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster*")) BY Web.src, Web.dest, Web.url, Web.user, Web.http_user_agent | `drop_dm_object_name(Web)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
Browser-spawned executable/installer drop within 5 min of TDS site contact AIDelivery High
Time-window correlation between a browser visit to a TDS / fake-tool domain and a fresh .exe/.msi/.dll/.zip dropped into Downloads/Temp by that same browser process. Catches the click-handoff step where the CloudFront JS staging layer converts a 'Download' click into a TDS-gated payload. Rationale: The article describes the 'Download' button click as a click-interception handoff via CloudFront JS to a TDS. A 5-minute browser→file-drop window keyed off contact with one of the 8 named domains converts the noisy 'browser dropped a file' signal into a high-fidelity TDS-delivery signal. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/ • https://www.fullstory.com/blog/
ATT&CKT1189 T1204.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Web.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • User legitimately browses TI-blog post that embeds one of the IOC domains as a link, then downloads an unrelated PDF in same window
  • Threat-hunter detonating samples in a non-isolated VM
  • Browser pre-fetch caching a TDS resource without an actual user click
  • Browser extension auto-update during a tab visit
Suppression filter
| where not(FileName endswith ".pdf" or FileName endswith ".png" or FileName endswith ".jpg")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the dropped file's SHA256 against VirusTotal/internal sandbox and the FileOriginUrl/Url field on the join — the article notes hovering shows a legitimate URL but the download path is intercepted, so compare displayed-link vs actual-origin. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill any child processes of the dropped binary, snapshot Downloads/Temp/Roaming and remove the file. 3) Hunt: sweep for the same SHA256 across the fleet, expand TDSDomains list to any sibling CloudFront hosts seen, and pivot on the user account for OAuth token and crypto-wallet access.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let TDSDomains = dynamic(["grpcurl.com","ghidralite.com","dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net","d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net","oundhertobeconisist.org","trkscope.xyz","file-enter-web.com","realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster"]);
let TDSTouches = DeviceNetworkEvents
  | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where RemoteUrl has_any (TDSDomains)
  | project TouchTime=Timestamp, DeviceId, DeviceName, RemoteUrl;
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\")
| where FileName endswith ".exe" or FileName endswith ".msi" or FileName endswith ".dll" or FileName endswith ".zip" or FileName endswith ".js"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| join kind=inner TDSTouches on DeviceId
| where Timestamp between (TouchTime .. TouchTime + 5m)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256, FileOriginUrl, RemoteUrl, TouchTime
| order by Timestamp desc
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let TDSDomains = dynamic(["grpcurl.com","ghidralite.com","dcbbwymp1bhif.cloudfront.net","d3jzqhqvnvdy34.cloudfront.net","oundhertobeconisist.org","trkscope.xyz","file-enter-web.com","realcubeoyogenmyfire.monster"]);
let TDSTouches = ImWebSession
  | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
  | where Url has_any (TDSDomains) or DstHostname has_any (TDSDomains)
  | project TouchTime=TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, Url;
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\")
| where TargetFileExtension in~ ("exe","msi","dll","zip","js","msix")
| where ActingProcessName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| join kind=inner TDSTouches on DvcHostname
| where TimeGenerated between (TouchTime .. TouchTime + 5m)
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSHA256, Url

SessionGate final-stage rundll32 spawning cmd.exe to fetch and silently execute next-stage payload AIInstallation High
Detects the SessionGate end-of-chain behaviour described in the article: a DLL loaded via rundll32.exe spawning cmd.exe to download and silently execute the unique-per-client next-stage malware. Specifically targets rundll32 living under user-writable paths (\AppData\, \Users\Public\) with cmd.exe carrying URL / download-utility tokens. Rationale: The article explicitly states the final DLL '...downloading and silently executing the next-stage malware via cmd.exe.' Pinning the detection on rundll32→cmd.exe with download-utility tokens or a user-writable parent path is article-specific and not covered by generic rundll32 abuse rules. The legitimate-pattern allowlist (printui, Control_RunDLL, mshtml PrintHTML) is the standard suppressor. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1218/011/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/
ATT&CKT1218.011 T1059.003 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT scripts using rundll32 launchers that legitimately call cmd.exe for URL launches (rare)
  • Software installers using rundll32 wrappers (some MSIs use rundll32 → cmd in temp)
  • Endpoint management agents that invoke cmd from a DLL loader
  • Browser/IME PrintHTML / Control_RunDLL invocations (already suppressed)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Windows\System32\", @"\Windows\SysWOW64\", @"\Program Files\", @"\Program Files (x86)\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull InitiatingProcessSHA256 (the DLL) and SHA256 (cmd.exe is benign, but the URL on the cmd line and any subsequent downloaded file matter); resolve and reputation-check the URL, hash the downloaded file. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the rundll32 chain and any spawned processes, terminate any persistence registry entries created in the same minute. 3) Hunt: sweep org for the DLL SHA256 and the loader's parent process tree (likely browser → installer → rundll32); pivot on the URL host across DeviceNetworkEvents for the past 30 days.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "rundll32.exe"
| where FileName =~ "cmd.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","curl ","certutil","bitsadmin","powershell","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where not(InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("printui.dll","shell32.dll,Control_RunDLL","mshtml.dll,PrintHTML"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\rundll32.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\\cmd.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","curl ","certutil","bitsadmin","powershell","Invoke-WebRequest","iwr ")
   or ParentProcessName has_any (@"\AppData\Local\Temp\", @"\AppData\Roaming\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where not(ParentProcessName has_any ("printui.dll","Control_RunDLL"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SessionGate rundll32 Spawning cmd.exe With Download Utility From User-Writable Path

level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @ParentImage:(*\\rundll32.exe OR *\\RUNDLL32.EXE) @Image:(*\\cmd.exe OR *\\CMD.EXE) AND (@CommandLine:(*http\:\/\/* OR *https\:\/\/* OR *curl* OR *certutil* OR *bitsadmin* OR *powershell* OR *Invoke-WebRequest*) OR @ParentCommandLine:(*\\AppData\\Local\\Temp\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\* OR *\\Users\\Public\\*))

| (regex("(?i)(http://|https://|curl |certutil|bitsadmin|powershell|Invoke-WebRequest|iwr )", field=CommandLine) OR regex("(?i)\\\\(AppData\\\\(Local|Roaming)|Users\\\\Public)\\\\", field=ParentCommandLine))
| NOT regex("(?i)(printui\.dll|shell32\.dll,Control_RunDLL|mshtml\.dll,PrintHTML)", field=ParentCommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())

Remus/Lumma Stealer browser-credential and crypto-wallet directory enumeration AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts for a single non-browser process touching three or more files across Chrome/Edge/Firefox/Brave Login Data stores AND/OR Exodus/Electrum/Atomic/Ledger Live/Coinomi/Bitcoin/Zcash wallet directories. Targets the Remus Stealer behaviour (article: 'steal data from more than 20 browsers...cryptocurrency wallets, two-factor authentication tools, and password managers'). Rationale: Article explicitly lists Remus Stealer's targets: 'more than 20 browsers, hundreds of browser extensions and applications, cryptocurrency wallets, two-factor authentication tools, and password managers'. The composite test — same non-browser process touching ≥3 distinct credential/wallet artefacts in a short window — is the canonical stealer fan-out signature and is robust to whichever variant of Remus/Lumma is delivered. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/software/S1167/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/
ATT&CKT1555.003 T1539 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Backup software (Acronis, Veeam Endpoint, Crashplan) scanning user profiles
  • Antivirus full scan touching Login Data SQLite databases
  • Browser-extension password manager performing a sync (covered by allowlist)
  • Forensic tool / DFIR live-response collection
  • Legitimate browser-profile migration tool (Mozilla profile import, Chrome → Edge migration)
Suppression filter
| where not(InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Program Files\Acronis\", @"\Program Files\Veeam\", @"\Program Files (x86)\Acronis\", @"\ProgramData\Microsoft\Windows Defender\"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the suspect process's SHA256, parent chain, and the network destinations it reached afterwards; correlate to TDS domain contact in UC1 for the same host. 2) Contain: isolate the host, force the user to rotate every credential stored in those browsers, kill active crypto-wallet sessions and rotate seed phrases where the user can confirm them; preserve a memory image before reimaging. 3) Hunt: dump and triage the C2 callback (often Lumma-family panels — check abuse.ch ThreatFox for Lumma config domain patterns), sweep DeviceNetworkEvents for similar callbacks across the fleet, and pivot on the SHA256 in VirusTotal for clustering.
let WindowDays = 7d;
let WalletPaths = dynamic([@"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Atomic\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Ledger Live\",@"\AppData\Local\Coinomi\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Zcash\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Bitcoin\"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data",@"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Login Data",@"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles",@"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\Default\Login Data"]);
let LegitProcs = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","svchost.exe","Bitwarden.exe","1Password.exe"]);
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(WindowDays)
| where FolderPath has_any (WalletPaths) or FolderPath has_any (CredPaths)
| where not(InitiatingProcessFileName in~ (LegitProcs))
| summarize FilesTouched=dcount(strcat(FolderPath, FileName)),
            SamplePaths=make_set(strcat(FolderPath, FileName), 10),
            FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp)
            by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| where FilesTouched >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
let WindowDays = 7d;
let WalletPaths = dynamic([@"\AppData\Roaming\Exodus\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Electrum\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Atomic\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Ledger Live\",@"\AppData\Local\Coinomi\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Zcash\",@"\AppData\Roaming\Bitcoin\"]);
let CredPaths = dynamic([@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\Default\Login Data",@"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\Default\Login Data",@"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles",@"\BraveSoftware\Brave-Browser\User Data\Default\Login Data"]);
let LegitProcs = dynamic(["chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","explorer.exe","SearchIndexer.exe","MsMpEng.exe","svchost.exe","Bitwarden.exe","1Password.exe"]);
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(WindowDays)
| where TargetFilePath has_any (WalletPaths) or TargetFilePath has_any (CredPaths)
| where not(ActingProcessName in~ (LegitProcs))
| summarize FilesTouched=dcount(TargetFilePath),
            SamplePaths=make_set(TargetFilePath, 10),
            FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine
| where FilesTouched >= 3
| order by LastSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:(11 OR 23) @TargetFilename:(*\\AppData\\Roaming\\Exodus\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\Electrum\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\Atomic\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\Ledger?Live\\* OR *\\AppData\\Local\\Coinomi\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\Zcash\\* OR *\\AppData\\Roaming\\Bitcoin\\* OR *\\Chrome\\User?Data\\Default\\Login?Data* OR *\\Edge\\User?Data\\Default\\Login?Data* OR *\\Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles* OR *\\Brave-Browser\\User?Data\\Default\\Login?Data*) -@Image:(*\\chrome.exe OR *\\msedge.exe OR *\\firefox.exe OR *\\brave.exe OR *\\explorer.exe OR *\\SearchIndexer.exe OR *\\MsMpEng.exe)
#event_simpleName=/^(FileWritten|FileOpenInfo)$/ TargetFileName=/\\(AppData\\(Roaming|Local)\\(Exodus|Electrum|Atomic|Ledger Live|Coinomi|Zcash|Bitcoin)|Chrome\\User Data\\Default\\Login Data|Edge\\User Data\\Default\\Login Data|Mozilla\\Firefox\\Profiles|Brave-Browser\\User Data\\Default\\Login Data)/i
| NOT ContextImageFileName=/\\(chrome|msedge|firefox|brave|explorer|SearchIndexer|MsMpEng|svchost)\.exe$/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName], function=count(field=TargetFileName, distinct=true, as=FilesTouched))
| FilesTouched >= 3

AnimateClipper ClickFix paste-to-run via explorer.exe spawning mshta/powershell/cmd AIExploitation High
Detects the ClickFix delivery pattern used by AnimateClipper where the lure tricks the user into pasting a malicious command into the Windows Run dialog, producing an explorer.exe → mshta.exe/powershell.exe/cmd.exe chain carrying URL or base64 tokens. Pinned to the clipboard-paste characteristics described in the article. Rationale: Article calls out AnimateClipper as 'delivered by means of a ClickFix lure'. ClickFix's canonical artefact is explorer.exe (the Run-dialog host) as parent of an interpreter or LOLBin with a URL or base64-encoded payload on the cmd line — a tight signature that is article-specific, not the generic encoded-PowerShell rule. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1204/004/ • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/
ATT&CKT1204.004 T1059.001 T1218.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer testing PowerShell one-liners from the Run dialog
  • IT admin manually pasting a remediation script
  • Software installer that shells out via explorer (rare)
  • Sysadmin demonstrating a remote-management one-liner during a screen share
Suppression filter
| where not(AccountName endswith "$")
| where not(AccountName in~ ("system","local service","network service"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: capture the full CommandLine and decode any -EncodedCommand / FromBase64String payload; resolve the URL and hash any file dropped. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the process tree, freeze the user's clipboard manager logs if available, and reset clipboard contents (the article notes AnimateClipper hijacks clipboard wallet addresses — sweep recent clipboard captures). 3) Hunt: pivot on the user's recent crypto transactions (if known) for address-substitution evidence, sweep the fleet for the same encoded payload pattern over the past 14 days, and check whether the same user also hit any TDS domain from UC1 in the prior 30 minutes.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "explorer.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("mshta.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","FromBase64String","DownloadString","DownloadFile","IEX","Invoke-Expression","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","javascript:","mshtml:","Set-Clipboard","hidden")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\\explorer.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\\mshta.exe","\\powershell.exe","\\pwsh.exe","\\cmd.exe","\\wscript.exe","\\cscript.exe")
| where CommandLine has_any ("http://","https://","FromBase64String","DownloadString","DownloadFile","IEX","Invoke-Expression","-EncodedCommand","-enc ","javascript:","mshtml:","Set-Clipboard","hidden")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Suspicious browser extension installation Installation Medium
Side-loaded / unsigned extensions, often masquerading as wallets, productivity tools.
ATT&CKT1176
Data sourcesEndpoint.Registry DeviceRegistryEvents
DeviceRegistryEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

High

Hackers Spied on a Stock Exchange Executive's Outlook Mailbox for Five Months

The Hacker News
2026-06-04 14 use cases 6 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Unknown attackers spent at least five months inside the Outlook mailbox of a senior executive at a major global stock exchange, copying the inbox out in small, repeated batches and routing it through Dropbox and OneDrive so the traffic blended into normal cloud activity. Symantec and Carbon Black's Threat Hunter Team reported the campaign this week. This points to espionage, not a money grab:

ATT&CKT1053.005 T1190 T1195.002 T1528 T1555.003 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Hackers Spied on a Stock Exchange Executive's Outlook Mailbox for Five Months
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst mailbox library loaded by non-Outlook process · [LLM] Scheduled task masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive system service · Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] FRPC (Fast Reverse Proxy client) execution by config-file argument
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] PST exported by non-Outlook binary with password and date-range CLI flags · [LLM] curl/non-browser binary uploading to Dropbox or OneDrive personal API endpoints · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant
Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst mailbox library loaded by non-Outlook process AIInstallation High
Hunts for the Aspose .NET library — which the Symantec/Carbon Black report identifies as the core of the attacker's mailbox stealer — being loaded by any process other than legitimate Outlook utilities. Aspose.Email and Aspose.Pst are the modules that read OST and write PST; their use outside Outlook/scanpst is highly anomalous on an executive endpoint. Rationale: Aspose.Email/Aspose.Pst are the specific libraries the article names as the heart of the mailbox stealer; loading them outside Outlook/scanpst is high-fidelity. Cross-checked Aspose product naming on the vendor site and Symantec's WastedLocker/Cl0p style write-ups, which use the same library identifiers. Cross-checked against: • https://docs.aspose.com/email/net/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/001/
ATT&CKT1114.001 T1005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Veritas Enterprise Vault / MailStore Server using Aspose.Email for archive ingestion
  • Custom e-discovery scripts in IT/Legal that read PSTs at scale
  • Aspose-based mail-merge or marketing tools running on workstations
  • Microsoft 365 migration utilities (third-party PST-to-Exchange-Online tooling)
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName !in~ ("Veritas Technologies LLC", "MailStore Software GmbH", "Quest Software Inc.", "Quadrotech Solutions")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the parent process tree and SHA256 of the loading binary; check whether the host runs a sanctioned archive/migration tool (Veritas, MailStore, Quadrotech). Validate the loading EXE is signed and resides in Program Files. Step 2 — Contain: if unsigned or in %ProgramData%/%AppData%/%Temp%, isolate the host via Defender Live Response and capture the binary plus any PST files in the working directory. Suspend the executive's Outlook session and rotate the user's mailbox export tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: enumerate DeviceFileEvents on the host for .pst writes in the last 180 days; pivot on InitiatingProcessSHA256 across the fleet to find sibling deployments; check for outbound flows from the same process to Dropbox/OneDrive endpoints (UC5).
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst") or FolderPath has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe", "olmapi32.dll")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
WindowsEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 7
| where EventData has_any ("Aspose.Email", "Aspose.Pst")
| where EventData !has "OUTLOOK.EXE" and EventData !has "scanpst.exe" and EventData !has "scanost.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Provider, EventID, EventData
title: Aspose Mailbox Library Loaded by Non-Outlook Process
id: 5c7d2e3a-9b4f-4a12-bd1a-1c2e3f4a5b6c
description: Detects Aspose.Email or Aspose.Pst .NET libraries being loaded by a process other than Outlook or PST repair tools, a signature behaviour of the stock-exchange-executive mailbox stealer reported by Symantec.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1114.001
  - attack.t1005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    ImageLoaded|contains:
      - 'Aspose.Email'
      - 'Aspose.Pst'
  filter_legit:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\outlook.exe'
      - '\scanpst.exe'
      - '\scanost.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter_legit
falsepositives:
  - Third-party mail-archive / e-discovery tools (Veritas, MailStore) that legitimately use Aspose
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:7 (@ImageLoaded:(*Aspose.Email* OR *aspose.email* OR *Aspose.Pst* OR *aspose.pst*)) -@Image:(*\\outlook.exe OR *\\OUTLOOK.EXE OR *\\scanpst.exe OR *\\scanost.exe)
#event_simpleName=ClassifiedModuleLoad OR #event_simpleName=ImageHash
| ImageFileName=/(Aspose\.Email|Aspose\.Pst)/i
| NOT (ContextImageFileName=/\\(outlook|scanpst|scanost)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ContextImageFileName, ImageFileName], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name!=outlook.exe Processes.process_name!=scanpst.exe Processes.process_name!=scanost.exe (Processes.process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name!=outlook.exe Processes.process_name!=scanpst.exe Processes.process_name!=scanost.exe (Processes.process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*") OR Processes.parent_process IN ("*Aspose.Email*","*Aspose.Pst*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
PST exported by non-Outlook binary with password and date-range CLI flags AIActions on Objectives High
Detects file writes of .pst files by a process that is not Outlook/scanpst when the launching command line carries password or date-range arguments. This is the article-specific operational pattern: the attacker's Aspose-wrapped tool was 'run each time with a password and a date-range flag' to slice the mailbox into bi-weekly chunks. Rationale: Both the file shape (.pst created by a non-Outlook process) and the CLI argument shape (password + date range) come directly from the article's description of how the attacker ran the tool eight times between Nov 2025 and Feb 2026. The combination is what makes it high-fidelity — either signal alone is too noisy. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1114/001/
ATT&CKT1114.001 T1560.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Sanctioned M&A or e-discovery PST exports run by IT (e.g. New-MailboxExportRequest spawning helper processes)
  • Migration suites such as Quest On Demand / BitTitan MigrationWiz writing PSTs during cutover
  • Backup software (Veeam Plug-in for Microsoft 365) producing PST files
  • User running Outlook File > Export to PST through a non-Outlook helper invoked by a managed deployment script
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: capture InitiatingProcessSHA256 and confirm signer; pivot the file path — exports to %ProgramData%, %AppData%, %Temp% or hidden user dirs are far more suspicious than a Documents folder. Pull file size and check if mailbox export was scheduled. Step 2 — Contain: isolate the host, kill the process, preserve the PST and binary for forensic review. Disable the user's mailbox export permission and revoke Outlook OAuth tokens. Step 3 — Hunt: look back 12 months for prior PST writes by the same SHA256; pivot to DeviceImageLoadEvents for Aspose libraries (UC1); search DeviceNetworkEvents for outbound Dropbox/OneDrive uploads from the same process (UC5).
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".pst"
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated", "FileModified")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe", "olmapi32.dll")
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-password", "/password", "-pwd", "/pwd", "-startdate", "-enddate", "/startdate", "/enddate", "-from", "-to", "-range", "/range", "-since")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FileName, FolderPath, FileSize, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName endswith ".pst"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("outlook.exe", "scanpst.exe", "scanost.exe")
| where ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("-password", "/password", "-pwd", "/pwd", "-startdate", "-enddate", "/startdate", "/enddate", "-from", "-to", "-range", "/range", "-since")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, TargetFileSize, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, TargetFileSHA256
title: PST Export by Non-Outlook Binary with Password and Date-Range Flags
id: 7e9a8b2c-3d4f-4a5b-9c1d-2e3f4a5b6c7d
description: Detects creation/modification of .pst files by a process other than Outlook/scanpst when the launching command line carries password or date-range flags - matches the bi-weekly mailbox-slice pattern from the stock exchange espionage campaign.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.collection
  - attack.t1114.001
  - attack.t1560.001
logsource:
  category: file_event
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_pst:

  - Sanctioned mailbox migration tooling (e.g. third-party PST exporters used during M&A)
level: high
source:windows.sysmon ((@EventID:11 @TargetFilename:*.pst) AND (@CommandLine:(*-password* OR *\/password* OR *-startdate* OR *-enddate* OR *\/startdate* OR *\/enddate*))) -@Image:(*\\outlook.exe OR *\\OUTLOOK.EXE OR *\\scanpst.exe OR *\\scanost.exe)
#event_simpleName=FileWritten TargetFileName=/\.pst$/i
| join({#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 CommandLine=/(-|\/)(password|pwd|startdate|enddate|range|since)/i NOT ImageFileName=/\\(outlook|scanpst|scanost)\.exe$/i}, field=ContextProcessId, key=TargetProcessId, include=[ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData])
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, TargetFileName], function=count())

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_name="*.pst" Filesystem.action IN ("created","modified") by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.user Filesystem.file_path Filesystem.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | join type=inner process_guid [| tstats summariesonly=false values(Processes.process) as cmdline values(Processes.process_name) as proc_name from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name!=outlook.exe Processes.process_name!=scanpst.exe (Processes.process="*password*" OR Processes.process="*startdate*" OR Processes.process="*enddate*" OR Processes.process="*-range*") by Processes.process_guid | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`] | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
Scheduled task masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive system service AIInstallation Medium
Hunts for schtasks.exe /create operations naming the task after Adobe, Lenovo or OneDrive when the parent process is not the corresponding genuine installer/updater. The Symantec write-up explicitly calls out scheduled tasks 'posing as Adobe, Lenovo and OneDrive system services' as the persistence layer. Rationale: The article explicitly names Adobe, Lenovo and OneDrive as the three vendors the attacker impersonated in scheduled-task names. Combining the schtasks /create command with those exact brand strings and a non-vendor parent process produces an article-specific pivot rather than a generic schtasks rule. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1053/005/ • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1036/005/
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Custom IT/imaging scripts that recreate vendor update tasks after a base image deploy
  • Endpoint management agents (Intune, SCCM, Tanium) rebuilding Adobe Reader or OneDrive update tasks
  • PowerShell-based GPO scripts that template scheduled tasks during user logon
  • Software repackagers (PSAppDeployToolkit) creating tasks during managed Adobe installs
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$" and InitiatingProcessAccountName !in~ ("system", "local service", "network service")
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: dump the full schtasks XML (`schtasks /query /tn <name> /xml`); inspect the action binary path, run-as principal, and trigger. Real Adobe tasks live under %ProgramFiles%; attacker binaries usually sit in %ProgramData%, %AppData% or C:\Windows\Temp. Step 2 — Contain: delete the task with `schtasks /delete /tn <name> /f`, kill the registered binary, isolate the host. Capture the binary referenced by the action for analysis. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot on the binary SHA256 across the fleet; pull DeviceProcessEvents for any process running as SYSTEM with an Adobe/OneDrive-looking name from a non-Program-Files path (overlaps the article's two SYSTEM masqueraders); review AsepValueUpdate for sibling Run-key persistence.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "schtasks.exe"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("/create", "-create")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Adobe", "Lenovo", "OneDrive")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("setup.exe", "msiexec.exe", "AdobeARM.exe", "Adobe_Updater.exe", "AdobeUpdateService.exe", "OneDriveSetup.exe", "OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe", "LenovoUpdate.exe", "SystemUpdate.exe", "trustedinstaller.exe")
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Adobe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files (x86)\Adobe" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Microsoft OneDrive" and InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files\Lenovo"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\schtasks.exe"
| where CommandLine has_any ("/create", "-create")
| where CommandLine has_any ("Adobe", "Lenovo", "OneDrive")
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\setup.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\msiexec.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\AdobeARM.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\OneDriveSetup.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\LenovoUpdate.exe"
| where ParentProcessName !endswith @"\trustedinstaller.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, CommandLine, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
title: Scheduled Task Masquerading as Adobe/Lenovo/OneDrive Service
id: 8a1b2c3d-4e5f-4a6b-9c1d-3e4f5a6b7c8d
description: Detects schtasks.exe /create commands whose task name impersonates Adobe, Lenovo, or OneDrive system services when the parent is not the corresponding vendor installer - matches the persistence masquerade in the Symantec stock-exchange espionage report.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/06/04
tags:
  - attack.persistence
  - attack.t1053.005
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_proc:
    Image|endswith: '\schtasks.exe'
    CommandLine|contains:
      - '/create'
      - '-create'
  selection_name:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'Adobe'
      - 'Lenovo'
      - 'OneDrive'
  filter_legit_parent:
    ParentImage|endswith:
      - '\setup.exe'
      - '\msiexec.exe'
      - '\AdobeARM.exe'
      - '\OneDriveSetup.exe'
      - '\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe'
      - '\LenovoUpdate.exe'
      - '\trustedinstaller.exe'
  condition: selection_proc and selection_name and not filter_legit_parent
falsepositives:
  - In-house IT scripts re-creating Adobe/OneDrive update tasks via PowerShell
level: medium
source:windows.security @EventID:4688 @Image:(*\\schtasks.exe OR *\\SCHTASKS.EXE) @CommandLine:(*\/create* OR *-create*) @CommandLine:(*Adobe* OR *Lenovo* OR *OneDrive*) -@ParentImage:(*\\AdobeARM.exe OR *\\OneDriveSetup.exe OR *\\OneDriveStandaloneUpdater.exe OR *\\LenovoUpdate.exe OR *\\trustedinstaller.exe OR *\\msiexec.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\schtasks\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(\/|-)create/i
| CommandLine=/(Adobe|Lenovo|OneDrive)/i
| NOT (ParentBaseFileName=/^(setup|msiexec|AdobeARM|Adobe_Updater|OneDriveSetup|OneDriveStandaloneUpdater|LenovoUpdate|trustedinstaller)\.exe$/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe (Processes.process="*/create*" OR Processes.process="*-create*") (Processes.process="*Adobe*" OR Processes.process="*Lenovo*" OR Processes.process="*OneDrive*") Processes.parent_process_name!=setup.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=msiexec.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=AdobeARM.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=OneDriveSetup.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=LenovoUpdate.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name=schtasks.exe (Processes.process="*/create*" OR Processes.process="*-create*") (Processes.process="*Adobe*" OR Processes.process="*Lenovo*" OR Processes.process="*OneDrive*") Processes.parent_process_name!=setup.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=msiexec.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=AdobeARM.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=OneDriveSetup.exe Processes.parent_process_name!=LenovoUpdate.exe by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
FRPC (Fast Reverse Proxy client) execution by config-file argument AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts for execution of frpc.exe or any renamed binary running with the distinctive FRPC config-file argument pattern. Symantec's published indicator set explicitly lists FRPC as the tunneling tool used in the intrusion kit alongside the mailbox stealer. Rationale: FRPC is named outright in the Symantec indicator bundle. Its config file is canonically frpc.ini (or .toml in newer builds) — covering both the binary name and the config-arg pattern catches renamed-binary variants used to evade naive name-only rules. Cross-checked against the public fatedier/frp GitHub repo for argument conventions. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/fatedier/frp • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1572/
ATT&CKT1572 T1090
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Authorised red-team operators running FRP during a sanctioned engagement
  • Developers using FRP for legitimate NAT traversal in lab environments
  • IoT/edge-device fleet management tools that bundle FRP for remote access
  • Self-hosted homelab / remote desktop bridges installed by power users on BYOD
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: dump the frpc config file (path is in the -c argument); record server_addr and server_port — that's the attacker's relay. Validate the SHA256 against VirusTotal. Step 2 — Contain: kill the FRPC process tree, block the discovered server_addr at the perimeter, isolate the host. Preserve the config file plus any sibling frps/frpc binaries. Step 3 — Hunt: search DeviceNetworkEvents fleet-wide for outbound TCP to the server_addr/port; pivot SHA256 across endpoints; review AsepValueUpdate and scheduled tasks (UC3) for FRPC persistence wrappers; correlate with credential-dumping tooling (Secretsdump, SharpDecryptPwd) named in the Symantec indicator bundle.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "frpc.exe"
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("frpc.ini", "frpc.toml", "frpc.yaml")
    or ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s+-c\s+\S*frpc\.(ini|toml|yaml)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256, MD5
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName endswith @"\frpc.exe"
    or CommandLine has_any ("frpc.ini", "frpc.toml", "frpc.yaml")
    or CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)\s+-c\s+\S*frpc\.(ini|toml|yaml)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
title: FRPC Fast Reverse Proxy Client Execution
id: 9b2c3d4e-5f6a-4b7c-9d2e-4f5a6b7c8d9e
description: Detects execution of frpc.exe or any binary invoked with the FRPC config-file argument shape, used as the tunneling tool in the stock-exchange espionage intrusion kit reported by Symantec.
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/06/hackers-spied-on-stock-exchange.html
  - https://github.com/fatedier/frp

logsource:

detection:
  selection_image:
    Image|endswith: '\frpc.exe'
  selection_cli:
    CommandLine|contains:
      - 'frpc.ini'
      - 'frpc.toml'
      - 'frpc.yaml'
  condition: selection_image or selection_cli
falsepositives:
  - Authorised red-team / pentest engagement using FRP
  - Developers using FRP for legitimate NAT-traversal in test labs
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 (@Image:(*\\frpc.exe OR *\\FRPC.EXE) OR @CommandLine:(*frpc.ini* OR *frpc.toml* OR *frpc.yaml*))
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| (ImageFileName=/\\frpc\.exe$/i OR CommandLine=/frpc\.(ini|toml|yaml)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine, SHA256HashData], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=frpc.exe OR Processes.process="*frpc.ini*" OR Processes.process="*frpc.toml*" OR Processes.process="*-c ./frpc*" OR Processes.process="*-c frpc.*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name=frpc.exe OR Processes.process="*frpc.ini*" OR Processes.process="*frpc.toml*" OR Processes.process="*-c ./frpc*" OR Processes.process="*-c frpc.*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_hash | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`
curl/non-browser binary uploading to Dropbox or OneDrive personal API endpoints AIActions on Objectives High
Detects curl, wget or other non-browser executables making outbound connections to Dropbox API hosts or OneDrive personal endpoints. Matches the article's exfiltration mechanic — the attacker pulled a Dropbox API token, uploaded with curl, and used OneDrive Personal to blend into normal cloud traffic. Rationale: The article explicitly names curl + Dropbox API tokens for the exfil channel and OneDrive Personal as the alternative. Pairing those destinations with non-browser process initiators (which never legitimately need to hit personal-cloud APIs on a corporate executive's workstation) yields a tight, article-specific detection. Cross-checked against: • https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1567/002/ • https://www.dropbox.com/developers/documentation/http/documentation
ATT&CKT1567.002 T1071.001
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer using curl to test Dropbox API integrations during a feature build
  • Sanctioned data-pipeline scripts uploading to a corporate Dropbox Business tenant
  • PowerShell-based Intune/MEM scripts pulling content from a *.sharepoint.com tenant (but not personal OneDrive)
  • User syncing files via rclone to a personal Dropbox/OneDrive on a BYOD workstation
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessCommandLine !has "dropboxbusiness" and InitiatingProcessAccountUpn !endswith "@yourcorp.com"
Response runbook
Step 1 — Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine — Dropbox bearer tokens are usually inline (`Authorization: Bearer sl....`). If a token is present, treat it as compromised. Identify whether the destination is the corporate Dropbox Business tenant or a personal account. Step 2 — Contain: kill the process tree, isolate the host, revoke the captured Dropbox token via Dropbox admin console, block dropboxapi.com / dropboxusercontent.com at the egress for this host. Step 3 — Hunt: pivot the initiating process SHA256 fleet-wide; check DeviceFileEvents for staged PSTs or archives written by the same process minutes before the upload; review UrlClickEvents and EmailEvents for the user across the prior 6 months to spot the original delivery; correlate with UC1/UC2 to tie the upload to a mailbox export.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("curl.exe", "wget.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "rclone.exe")
| where RemoteUrl has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "files.dropbox.com", "dropboxusercontent.com", "onedrive.live.com", "storage.live.com", "my.microsoftpersonalcontent.com")
   or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "Authorization: Bearer", "Dropbox-API-Arg")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort, InitiatingProcessSHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where SrcUsername != ""
| where DstHostname has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "files.dropbox.com", "dropboxusercontent.com", "onedrive.live.com", "storage.live.com")
| join kind=inner (
    ImProcessCreate
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
    | where ActingProcessName in~ ("curl.exe", "wget.exe", "powershell.exe", "pwsh.exe", "certutil.exe", "bitsadmin.exe", "rclone.exe")
        or ActingProcessCommandLine has_any ("api.dropboxapi.com", "content.dropboxapi.com", "Dropbox-API-Arg")
) on $left.DvcHostname == $right.DvcHostname
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, SrcUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, DstHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
title: Non-Browser Binary Connecting to Dropbox or OneDrive Personal API
id: a3b4c5d6-7e8f-4a9b-9c1d-5e6f7a8b9c0d
description: Detects curl, wget, powershell or other non-browser executables establishing connections to Dropbox API or OneDrive personal endpoints, matching the article's curl-based Dropbox upload and OneDrive Personal exfiltration paths.

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
